title: Many Iowans Must Navigate a Maze to Vote
author: Alex Burness
content:
Raul Lara, a construction worker from the small town of Stanwood, is eager to
weigh in as Iowa elects its new governor next week. “I just want somebody to
run the damn state correctly,” he says.

He should be eligible to do so. Current state policy allows most any citizen
to vote so long as they aren’t serving a felony sentence, and Lara, who was
criminally convicted a couple of years ago over a dispute with neighbors,
finished his probation months ago.

However, Lara says that when he tried to register earlier this year, he was
turned away by his county elections office, which told him he needed to submit
a letter explaining why he was now eligible to vote. He enlisted the help of
an attorney, who submitted the letter but then was told that a state database
listed Lara, incorrectly, as still serving a felony sentence.

It took the attorney contacting different state and local offices multiple
times before Lara could finally register and obtain a mail ballot—a
convoluted, burdensome process that Lara says he couldn’t have navigated
without help.

As he readied to submit his ballot in late October, Lara told _Bolts_ that he
remained nervous; given the earlier mix-up, he doesn’t want to be accused of
voting illegally.

“I don’t know yet if my ballot is going to be good or not. We still don’t
know. They’ve never told us if it’s good or not,” he said. “I’m pretty mad.
I’m an American citizen and I’ve got rights to vote.”

Lara is far from the only Iowan unsure of their voting status this fall.
_Bolts_ spoke with others in the state who are caught up in a bureaucratic
maze or confused about their right to vote as they sought to cast ballots
after finishing their sentences. Lawyers who help them say that a lack of
clear guidance from state and local officials makes it a common problem, which
threatens to suppress civic engagement from would-be voters.

This is because Iowa has harsh, oft-changing rules for when people with
criminal convictions can regain the right to vote. It is one of just three
states, along with Kentucky and Virginia, where the state constitution
establishes that anyone convicted of any felony loses the right to vote for
life. Governor Kim Reynolds, a Republican [who herself has a past criminal
conviction](https://www.krqe.com/news/politics/iowa-governor-got-2nd-chance-
she-thinks-felons-should-too/), signed an [executive
order](https://boltsmag.org/iowa-governor-expands-voting-rights/) in 2020 that
made it so people regain their voting rights when they complete their
sentence, including terms of prison, probation, and parole.

The Sentencing Project [estimated](https://www.iowapublicradio.org/ipr-
news/2020-10-14/report-estimates-about-45-000-iowans-with-felony-convictions-
had-voting-rights-restored) at the time that some 45,000 people regained
voting rights at once as a result of that order.

But the order was followed by little public outreach and voter education.
State elections officials also say they’ve collected no data since 2020 on the
order’s effects.

Voting rights advocates and people who work in the criminal legal system say
many Iowans who have regained eligibility thanks to Reynolds’ actions still
have no idea where they stand—and often incorrectly believe that they cannot
vote because officials never told them they’re eligible, or gave them
inaccurate information when they asked.

“Even a lot of the ones who are interested in voting, they don’t know truly
what their status is,” said Bo James, director of the Iowa nonprofit Hip Hope,
and who has many clients and family members with past felony convictions.

The affected population skews disproportionately Black, as [racial
disparities](https://www.prisonpolicy.org/blog/2023/09/27/updated_race_data/)
in Iowa’s criminal legal system are among the highest in the nation. According
to the [ACLU of Iowa](https://www.aclu-ia.org/press-releases/iowa-found-
rank-7th-worst-prison-racial-disparities/), 25 percent of incarcerated Iowans
are Black, even though Black people make up just 4 percent of the state’s
population.

James thinks that the present murkiness around voting rights reinforces
people’s sense that their participation is unwanted; research
[shows](https://boltsmag.org/a-police-stop-is-enough-to-make-someone-less-
likely-to-vote/) even minor contact with the criminal legal system makes
people less likely to vote. “As long as they have any type of relationship
with the judicial system,” he told _Bolts_ , “they feel like they’re still
paying their penance and haven’t been fully restored to citizenship, and that
therefore they’re not deserving of that voting right.”

* * *

Some of the confusion, James and other experts say, stems from the particulars
of Reynolds’ executive order, which demand some navigation to determine
whether one’s rights have been restored.

For one thing, the order doesn’t cover everyone, maintaining lifetime
disenfranchisement for people convicted of a [class of
charges](https://www.legis.iowa.gov/docs/code/707.pdf) that includes homicide
and related offenses, such as manslaughter and voluntary manslaughter.

But more notably, while the order restores voting rights when someone has
“discharged his or her sentence,” many mistake this to include financial
obligations.

In fact, Iowa doesn’t require people to pay off court debt before regaining
their voting rights, in contrast to states like
[Florida](https://boltsmag.org/desantis-voter-arrests-amendment-4/) that
require people seeking to regain voting rights to pay fines, fees, or
restitution—a sort of poll tax that functionally excludes poorer residents.

Many people who work with Iowans with past convictions told _Bolts_ that those
covered by the Reynolds order—and some officials tasked with administering
it—often do not know this, leading some to believe they’re ineligible because
of outstanding costs.

“There is confusion at the individual level and at the state level about when
someone has discharged a court sentence,” said Alison Guernsey, who directs
the Federal Criminal Defense Clinic at the University of Iowa.

![](https://boltsmag.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Reynolds.jpg)Governor Kim
Reynolds, a Republican, issued an executive order in 2020 to restore voting
rights to most Iowans who have completed their sentence (photo via Iowa
governor/Facebook).

Some people in Iowa owe court costs that they will pay for the rest of their
lives. Sentences for certain convictions come with mandatory restitution of
more than $100,000—an amount so high as to be forever unattainable for many,
even if they’re on aggressive payment plans.

Guernsey said she’s observed that people with outstanding court costs “try to
avoid interacting with the state at all if they think it can possibly get them
in trouble.”

“So the default is that if you’re not sure, you don’t vote,” Guernsey said.
“The assumption is you aren't eligible and if someone hasn't told you that you
are, then you don't.”

Advocates and canvassers nationwide say it’s easiest for them to inform people
of their rights, and do so without fearing a costly error, when there is a
clear and unambiguous line in the sand—for instance, when they can tell people
that anyone can vote as long as they’re not incarcerated for a felony
conviction. That simple rule is currently in place in 23 states. Messaging is
even more straightforward in Maine, Vermont, and Washington, D.C., which don’t
strip anyone of the right to vote, even if they’re in prison.

But as the rules get more complicated, advocates find that even people who are
eligible often stay away from the polls for fear of breaking the law.

Confusion over Reynolds’ order can also extend beyond just those who were
covered by it. While the order also gave people with past convictions the
right to serve on a jury, Aaron Hawbaker, a public defender and Cedar Falls
city council member, told _Bolts_ that lawyers have had to remind judges and
prosecutors that someone shouldn’t be tossed from a jury pool simply because
they have a past conviction.

“We’ve had to educate judges time and again about the order,” Hawbaker said.

* * *

The true impact of Reynolds’ executive order is difficult to discern. Both her
office and the secretary of state’s office told _Bolts_ they don’t collect any
data on the number of people who regained the right to vote, or on
registration rates of those affected, making it hard to assess exactly where
the Reynolds reform is working and where it’s falling short.

The state also did very little to inform people with previous convictions
about the order or take steps to absolve any confusion over who could regain
their voting rights. The secretary of state’s office says it does not do any
targeted outreach to people with past convictions.

This is a common national problem. Even states with relatively permissive
disenfranchisement rules rarely do much in the way of data collection, or in
outreach to people unsure of their rights.

In Kentucky, when Governor Andy Beshear in 2019 ordered a mass restoration of
voting rights for people with past felonies, the state did not actually notify
the many thousands of people affected; seven years later, advocates there [are
still trying to spread the word](https://boltsmag.org/kentucky-voting-rights-
restoration/).

Iowans face the same issue. “People still have the belief that they can’t
vote, so they don’t try,” Hawbaker said.

Even those inclined to try to vote must frequently go it alone. Cardell James,
a formerly incarcerated man from Des Moines, told _Bolts_ he had to
investigate his own voting status after completing his sentence in 2021. “I
was happy when I could vote, but I never got told about it” by the state, he
said. “It’s all just word of mouth.”

Other Iowans with past criminal convictions told _Bolts_ they’ve struggled to
actually register and cast a ballot even after determining that Reynolds’
order granted them voting rights.

Lara, the Stanwood construction worker, said he would not have even attempted
to register if he hadn’t happened upon a story in local media about voting
rights. “Nobody told me anything before that,” he said. “My wife looked it up.
That made me feel pretty bad. It really pissed me off.”

Eric Tindal, the attorney who assisted Lara in correcting his erroneous
exclusion, says one underlying issue is that the state has not created any
easily accessible database that an election official could query to tell
someone who is inquiring whether they are eligible to vote.

Katarina Sostaric, spokesperson for the Iowa Judicial Branch, told _Bolts_
that the office “works very hard to ensure that criminal convictions are
reported accurately to the Iowa secretary of state” to prevent situations like
Lara’s. Sostaric said she could not comment on Lara’s case in particular, but
added, “Errors in processing a conviction are rare, and the Judicial Branch
takes steps to promptly correct them.”

Still, Tindal and other attorneys in Iowa say they’ve observed that local and
state systems sometimes do not communicate well, or accurately, as to the
status of someone who is or was finishing out a sentence.

“There's a whole lot of networks and apps going on that necessarily count on
people checking the right boxes at the right times,” Tindal said. ****“It’s
not just voting rights,” he added. “There are other things falling through the
cracks because we 're making public decisions that underfund all services.”
This public funding concern, which affects [local
budgets](https://www.iowapublicradio.org/ipr-news/2026-09-15/des-moines-city-
council-budget-cuts) as well, was accelerated by large tax cuts approved by
Reynolds in 2024.

The governor is retiring this year, meaning that whoever wins the election to
replace her in November will have the power to extend or modify her executive
order on voting rights—or rescind it.

_Bolts_ tried to interview the gubernatorial nominees, Republican Zach Lahn
and Democrat Rob Sand, on this topic, or to at least obtain position
statements. In an unsigned email, Lahn’s campaign vowed to respond weeks ago
but never did. Sand’s campaign manager, C.J. Petersen, referred _Bolts_ to a
campaign spokesperson, Emma O’Brien, who did not respond to repeated messages
asking for Sand’s views on the issue.

![](https://boltsmag.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/10/733831561_982257788136870_7248237770711252507_n-e1792774628898.jpg)Rob
Sand, the Democratic nominee for Iowa governor, told an advocacy organization
that he favors maintaining the current executive order in place and codifying
it into the state constitution (photo via Sand campaign/Facebook).

After an interview with _Bolts_ , Betty Andrews, who directs the Iowa-Nebraska
branch of the NAACP, and who helped lead advocacy for the Reynolds order six
years ago, sent letters to both candidates asking whether they would maintain
the rights restoration policy.

Sand’s campaign responded to Andrews to say that he would keep Reynolds’ order
in place, while Lahn’s campaign did not respond. (O’Brien, Sand’s
spokesperson, confirmed to _Bolts_ that they sent the responses.) Sand’s
campaign also said he’d use the governor’s platform to encourage eligible
Iowans with felony backgrounds to participate in elections, but did not
elaborate on how.

* * *

That Sand went much of the campaign without addressing Reynolds’ order, while
Lahn still hasn’t addressed it at all, is typical in a country where
politicians tend to shy from the topic of voting rights for people with past
convictions.

It’s also consistent with _Bolts_ ’ past reporting in Kentucky and Virginia,
the other states that hand governors sole authority over the voting rights of
anyone convicted of a felony.

When Beshear ran for re-election as Kentucky governor in 2023, Kentuckians
with past criminal convictions were [anxious](https://boltsmag.org/kentucky-
rights-restoration-governor-election-beshear-cameron/) about their voting
status, much like Iowans affected by Reynolds’ rights restoration order are
now. But neither Beshear nor his then-opponent discussed the topic during
their respective campaigns, and both declined to speak with _Bolts_ about it
while running.

The same story played out last year in Virginia’s gubernatorial election, with
neither candidate taking a public position on how they’d tackle voting rights
restoration, despite heated [legal and political
battles](https://boltsmag.org/readmission-acts-and-felony-disenfranchisement/)
around the issue in the state.

Abigail Spanberger, the Democrat who prevailed in that election, ended up
[restoring the rights of tens of thousands](https://boltsmag.org/virginia-
governor-restores-voting-rights/) of Virginians this summer, countering her
Republican predecessor’s [restrictive policies](https://boltsmag.org/virginia-
governor-rights-restoration-blocked-from-voting/). Even as she did so, some
affected Virginians told _Bolts_ they still weren’t sure where they stood, and
were nervous to try registering.

![](https://boltsmag.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Lahn-2400x1600.jpg)Zach
Lahn, the GOP nominee for Iowa governor, has not shared his position on the
issue of felony disenfranchisement (photo via Sand campaign/Facebook).

Voting rights advocates in these states that empower governors to pick and
choose the bounds of felony disenfranchisement are frustrated that they have
to wonder, cycle after cycle, whether and how the rules might change.

“We are keenly concerned,” Andrews said, of Iowa’s current moment. “We fought
for years to get here. This could be overturned or changed with one
administration.”

Advocates like her would like to see permanent changes to enshrine voting
rights into the state constitution, rather than leave them at a governor’s
mercy.

Virginia is [on the verge](https://boltsmag.org/virginia-constitutional-
amendment-to-repeal-lifetime-ban-on-voting/) of such a reform now: Voters
there will decide next week on a proposed constitutional amendment that would
automatically restore voting rights as soon as someone leaves prison.
(Spanberger says she supports the change.) Kentucky has for years debated a
related, though less sweeping step, but that effort has stalled out several
times, [including this
spring](https://ballotpedia.org/Kentucky_Restore_Voting_Rights_for_Certain_Convicted_Felons_Amendment_\(2026\)).

In Iowa, advocates have also spent many years pushing the GOP-controlled
legislature for a constitutional amendment, [to no
avail](https://iowacapitaldispatch.com/2020/06/17/reynolds-its-misleading-to-
say-senate-gop-broke-deal-on-felon-voting-rights/). In fact, Reynolds only
issued her 2020 order because the legislature had failed to put the matter to
voters.

“A constitutional amendment continues to be the only permanent solution to
this issue,” she wrote in her order.

In her letters to Lahn and Sand, Andrews specifically asked whether they’d
support such a reform. Sand’s campaign answered in a word: “Yes.”

But that sort of change may still be years away, at the earliest, leaving
people with past convictions to contend this voting season with a system that
is falling well short of the promise of the Reynolds order.

“This was supposed to be so much easier,” said Doren Walker, a formerly
incarcerated Iowan. “People are falling through the cracks.”

One night in Stanwood last week, Raul Lara was readying to submit his ballot
the following morning, hopeful that it would actually count.

“I’m worried about that,” he said. “And I am wondering if this is happening to
other people—people who have that same problem as me, blocking them from
voting.”
